Key Features: Self-describing schema-in-band packets; 8 primitives (int, dec, bool, str, seq, map, ref, null); A1-A3 axioms (composition, explicit typing, homogeneous sequences); R4-R7 rules (canonical key order, null-is-not-absence, namespaced versioning, lossless round-trip); L0-L3 conformance levels; SHA-256 integrity hash per document.
How to Use With 121XML / 121AI: This is the hub format. Every other row in this table is a spoke that gets a 121XML profile (e.g. https://spec.121.us/121xml/1.1/mcp-tool, .../onnx-model, .../mem0-memory, .../gguf-model) so objects from each ecosystem can be represented, hashed, and round-tripped inside the same object store.
Pros: No pre-shared schema needed at the receiver; tamper-evident via canonical hashing; new fields don't break old readers (R6); vendor-neutral by design; you own and control the spec.
Cons: More bytes on the wire than binary formats (verbose text/XML); zero existing tooling or ecosystem outside what you build; adoption depends entirely on you shipping working connectors and a certification story; unproven at scale.
Cost: Free / self-owned. Cost is entirely engineering time to build the serializer, profiles, and connectors.
How to Build a 121XML Connector: N/A -- this is the target format itself. Every other row describes how to build a connector INTO this format.

Key Features: JSON-RPC based; lets an LLM client discover and call tools/resources exposed by independent servers; official reference servers include a knowledge-graph Memory server (entities, relations, observations); ~10,000+ active public servers, 97M monthly SDK downloads (2026).
How to Use With 121XML / 121AI: Expose your 121XML object store as an MCP server so Claude, ChatGPT, or any MCP client can call tools like search_objects, get_object, create_object, merge_objects against your 121XML data -- without those clients knowing anything about 121XML internally.
Pros: Already the dominant tool-calling standard; free and open; huge existing client base (Claude, Cursor, VS Code, ChatGPT); building one MCP server exposes your data to every MCP client at once.
Cons: MCP's own data model is untyped/loose JSON -- you lose 121XML's type tags and hash unless you re-embed them as extra fields; protocol governs tool-calling, not long-term storage semantics; still evolving (spec has had several breaking revisions).
Cost: Free (open protocol, no licensing fee). Cost is hosting your own MCP server (compute) and dev time.
How to Build a 121XML Connector: 1) Define a 121XML profile per object type (e.g. contact, memory, agent-config). 2) Build an MCP server (Python or TypeScript SDK) with tools: get_object(id), search_objects(query), create_object(typed_fields), update_object(id, fields). 3) Inside each tool handler, serialize/deserialize through your 121XML parser (Pattern 1/2 in the Technical Reference) so every read/write is hash-verified and round-trip-checked. 4) Return MCP's required JSON shape to the client, with the 121XML hash included as a field for provenance.

Key Features: Vendor-neutral computation graph representation built on Protobuf; lets a model trained in PyTorch run in TensorFlow, ONNX Runtime, or edge devices without retraining; mature multi-year ecosystem, broad industry adoption.
How to Use With 121XML / 121AI: Represent an ONNX model's metadata (inputs, outputs, ops, opset version, producer) as a 121XML object -- e.g. a 121xml/1.1/onnx-model profile -- so a model's shape and provenance can sit in your object store and relationship graph alongside contacts, agents, and memories, even though the model weights themselves stay in .onnx binary form.
Pros: Already the closest real-world proof that 'any framework, any model' interchange works at scale; well-documented Protobuf schema; strong tooling (Netron viewer, ONNX Runtime) you can reuse rather than rebuild.
Cons: ONNX only covers the model graph/weights, not surrounding context (prompts, agent config, memory) -- 121XML would only wrap metadata, not replace the binary weight format; Protobuf (out-of-band schema) is architecturally the opposite of 121XML's in-band philosophy, so the two are complementary, not substitutable.
Cost: Free / open source (Apache 2.0). Cost is compute for any conversion/inference tooling you run.
How to Build a 121XML Connector: 1) Do not re-encode the weights -- keep the .onnx file as-is. 2) Parse the ONNX file's metadata (graph name, inputs/outputs with shapes and types, producer, opset) using the onnx Python package. 3) Map that metadata into a 121XML map object under a model-metadata profile, with a ref field pointing to the external .onnx file's location/hash. 4) Store this object in your 121XML store so the model becomes a node in your relationship graph; the round-trip test here is metadata-only (R7 applies to the 121XML wrapper, not the binary weights).

Category: Agent memory layer (open source + hosted platform)
Key Features: Flat key-value memory store, framework-agnostic (works with LangChain, CrewAI, AutoGen, custom loops); extracts facts from conversation and retrieves by semantic/keyword/entity match; optional graph memory add-on for entity relationships; 41,000 GitHub stars, 14M downloads.
How to Use With 121XML / 121AI: Use Mem0's SDK as one possible memory backend behind your 121XML memory profile: when Mem0 extracts and stores a fact, mirror it into a 121XML memory object (user/session/agent-scoped) so the same fact is queryable both through Mem0's API and through your own object store/graph UI.
Pros: Fastest way to get working agent memory without building extraction/retrieval logic yourself; Apache 2.0 open source option avoids lock-in; hosted platform has a real free tier for prototyping.
Cons: Flat schema is less expressive than Letta's tiered model if you need core/recall/archival distinctions later; hosted platform costs scale with memory count and retrieval calls; you still need to build the bridge into 121XML yourself -- no native 121XML support exists.
Cost: Open source: free (self-hosted). Hosted platform: Hobby free tier (10,000 memories, 1,000 retrieval calls/mo); Starter $19/mo; Growth $79/mo; Pro $249/mo (unlimited memories, graph memory); Enterprise custom.
How to Build a 121XML Connector: 1) Run Mem0 self-hosted (open source) or via hosted API. 2) On every memory.add() call, also serialize the same fact into a 121XML memory object (fields: subject-ref, predicate, object, source-session, confidence, __hash) and write it to your object store. 3) On retrieval, query Mem0 as usual for ranked results, then resolve each hit's ID against your 121XML store to pull the full typed, hashed record. 4) This gives you Mem0's retrieval quality with 121XML's provenance/round-trip guarantees on top.

Category: Local model weight file format (GGML/llama.cpp ecosystem)
Key Features: Binary format for fast-loading quantized model weights, designed for local/edge inference; single-file distribution with embedded metadata (architecture, tokenizer, quantization type); extensible without breaking old readers.
How to Use With 121XML / 121AI: Same pattern as ONNX: represent a GGUF file's header metadata (architecture, parameter count, quantization, context length, tokenizer info) as a 121XML object so locally-run models are inventoried and hash-tracked in your object store, even though inference still reads the raw GGUF file directly.
Pros: Free, open, and specifically designed for local-first / low-cost inference -- philosophically aligned with the 'local-first, your data stays yours' positioning already in your Nexus concept; single-file distribution is simple to hash and version.
Cons: Only covers weights + minimal metadata, no agent/memory/session concepts at all; smaller ecosystem than ONNX outside the llama.cpp world; quantization introduces lossy behavior that has nothing to do with 121XML's round-trip guarantee (don't conflate the two).
Cost: Free / open source. Cost is local compute (GPU/CPU) to run inference, no licensing fee for the format itself.
How to Build a 121XML Connector: 1) Read the GGUF file's key-value metadata header (architecture, quantization, vocab size, context length) using a GGUF parsing library. 2) Map that header into a 121XML map object under a local-model profile, with a ref to the file path/hash and a str field for quantization type. 3) Store alongside ONNX and other model-metadata objects in the same object store so local and cloud-runtime models appear as the same node type in the relationship graph, differentiated only by profile/tags.
